results.title: Runcrate: GPUs and a Model API
highlights:
- An instance is a machine with a named GPU, SSH, Jupyter, and VS Code in the browser. Ready images called crates, including Devbox, Finetune, and Inference, boot with the tools already installed. Runcrate says the image itself is not an extra charge on top of the machine.
- The model API is OpenAI-compatible at api.runcrate.ai/v1. Their pricing page, checked 22 October 2026, says 223 models sit behind it. One listed rate is DeepSeek V3.2 at $0.273 per million input tokens and $0.399 per million output tokens. Image models are mostly priced per image, and video per second.
- A storage volume keeps files after the GPU is deleted, then mounts on the next machine. The price is $0.03 per GB a month, from 10 GB to 10,000 GB, prepaid a week at a time. Delete it early and the unused days go back to the balance. Their docs say the files live on the instance disk at /workspace, and one volume attaches to one running instance at a time.
- An agent can drive it from the terminal. The documented Claude Code setup is one command: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user runcrate https://mcp.runcrate.ai/mcp. You then approve the login in the browser. There is no key to paste for that step.

## The from-price is the cheapest offer, not the only one

Runcrate publishes a price feed at runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing and says it refreshes every five minutes. The copy below is that feed at 13:00 UTC on 22 October 2026. It listed 17 GPU types. The low number is the cheapest offer in stock. The same chip is often listed higher.

- A4000: $0.20 to $1.04 an hour. That $0.20 floor is the cheapest line in the feed.
- A6000: $0.65 to $2.51 an hour. An October 19 launch replay on the homepage used an A6000 at $0.65 an hour, which matches today's floor, not every A6000 they list.
- H100 SXM: $5.17 to $7.79 an hour, and the feed only showed single-GPU offers.
- H200: $4.24 an hour, flat in this snapshot. It is the only GPU the feed marks as billed by the minute. The others in the feed are not marked that way.
- GAUDI2: $1.43 an hour, and only as an eight-GPU count.
- Eight-GPU counts also appear as on-demand offers for H200, A100, L40, and a few others. A reserved quote is a separate path, for a month or longer, several nodes, or a cluster an engineer sizes.

The same pricing page has a card saying $20 buys five hours on one H100 SXM. At the feed's cheapest H100 rate, $5.17 an hour, $20 is under four hours. This page does not decide which of those two numbers the cashier uses. Treat the feed as the list of offers, and the card as a slogan that did not match it.

## When the meter runs

- Billing starts when the instance reports running, and stops when you delete it. Boot time is not billed.
- Most GPUs bill by the second. Runcrate says a few bill in whole minutes, rounded up, and that rounding includes about 30 seconds of teardown after you delete. In the feed above, only the H200 was flagged as per-minute.
- You add $20 to $10,000 by card. A launch needs $10, or one hour of that machine, whichever is more. With auto-recharge on, the minimum they state is $10.
- Auto-recharge uses a floor you set from $20 to $5,000 and a refill target from $50 to $10,000. A declined card turns it off, and they email you.
- Under $1 they try auto-recharge, email you, and wait 15 minutes before deleting running instances. If the balance reaches minus $10, they say the wait can be shorter. Time already used is still billed.

...

The product is at runcrate.ai. Live GPU offers are the JSON at /api/gpu-pricing. The billing rules are on the pricing page. The origin post is on Hugging Face. The image on this page is Runcrate's wordmark banner, a drawing of stacked cards, not a screenshot of the console and not a Seailife test.

results.title: How to compare GPU cloud prices without fooling yourself - DEV Community
results.author: Runcrate
highlights:
"H100 from $X an hour" is the least useful number in a GPU price list. Two offers with the same headline can differ by a factor of two in what you pay at the end of the month, and two offers with very different headlines can come out the same.

We publish GPU prices at Runcrate, and other people's comparison sites read them, so I spend a lot of time looking at how a price turns into a bill. This is the checklist I use. It works for any provider, ours included. I'll use our public pricing endpoint for the examples because it's the data I can show you with a script, not because the method depends on it.

...

Runcrate's endpoint already reports per GPU-hour and needs no API key: 

```
import requests

data = requests.get("https://www.runcrate.ai/api/gpu-pricing").json()
print("fetched at", data["fetched_at"])

for g in data["gpus"]:
    s = g["specs"]
    per_gpu = s["num_gpus"] or 1
    print(
        f'{g["name"]:12} {g["vram"]:>6}  '
        f'${g["min_price_hr"]:.2f} to ${g["max_price_hr"]:.2f} per GPU-hr  '
        f'{g["available_options"]:>2} configs  GPUs per machine {g["gpu_counts"]}  '
        f'~{s["vcpus"] // per_gpu} vCPU / {s["memory_gb"] // per_gpu} GB RAM per GPU'
    )

```

Part of what it printed when I ran it (fetched at 2026-10-21T00:51 UTC): 

```
H100 SXM       80GB  $3.38 to $7.79 per GPU-hr   7 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 8]  ~20 vCPU / 128 GB RAM per GPU
A100 80GB      80GB  $1.76 to $4.26 per GPU-hr  12 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 8]  ~28 vCPU / 120 GB RAM per GPU
L40S           48GB  $1.14 to $1.95 per GPU-hr  10 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4, 8]  ~12 vCPU / 72 GB RAM per GPU
A6000          48GB  $0.65 to $2.51 per GPU-hr  18 configs  GPUs per machine [1, 2, 4]  ~28 vCPU / 58 GB RAM per GPU

```

Notice the ranges. One GPU model can have a dozen configurations with a 2x to 4x spread between them. A comparison that keeps only the minimum hides that the minimum might be one 8-GPU node in one region.

...

"A100" is two products (40 GB and 80 GB). "H100" is SXM or PCIe, with different memory bandwidth and interconnect. A "4090" with 24 GB will not hold the model your 48 GB card holds. Before comparing prices, match:

- VRAM (the endpoint has `vram` per GPU type)
- form factor and interconnect for multi-GPU work (`interconnect`, for example NVLink)
- GPU count per machine, because you can't split an 8-GPU node

...

## 6. Date every number 

GPU prices change weekly, sometimes daily. A comparison without a date is a guess. Put the fetch time next to every price (the endpoint returns `fetched_at` for that reason), and re-run your script rather than reusing last month's table.

...

Written with AI assistance. The script and prices above were run against the live endpoint on 2026-10-21.

results.title: RunPod Serverless GPU prices are up — B200 up about 25%, every tier higher | GPUJournal
highlights:
RunPod's Serverless GPU rates have risen on every tier, recorded between the Oct 26 and Nov 2, 2026 captures of its own pricing page: B200 $8.64 → $10.79 an hour is the largest move, up about 25%. RunPod announced nothing — the new figures are simply the ones live on runpod.io/pricing today, which we read first-hand on Nov 2.

...

What changed — the new figures read on RunPod's own pricing page (runpod.io/pricing) on Nov 2, 2026, against the figures captured from the same page on Oct 26, 2026: B300 $10.65 → $11.99 (up about 13%), B200 $8.64 → $10.79 (up about 25%), H200 $5.93 → $6.99 (up about 18%), H100 $4.79 → $5.39 (up about 13%), RTX 5090 $1.58 → $1.79 (up about 13%), RTX 4090 $1.10 → $1.34 (up about 22%), and the grouped L4 / A5000 / 3090 rate $0.69 → $0.75 (up about 9%). Every Serverless tier rose; none fell. On sourcing, plainly: the after-figures are RunPod's own page as we read it today; the before-figures are PricingSaaS Pulse's dated Oct 26 capture of that same page, because our own archive does not hold the October Serverless buckets — the comparison is recorded at pricingsaas.com/companies/runpod/diffs/2026W45. There is no RunPod announcement and no stated effective date; the honest date for the change is the window between the two captures.

...

What did not change: RunPod's Pods. Re-read on Nov 2, 2026, Pods Secure prices are exactly where they were — B300 $8.99, B200 $7.99, H200 $5.29, H100 SXM $3.99, A100 $1.79, L40S $1.09, RTX 5090 $1.19, RTX 4090 $0.89 and RTX PRO 6000 $2.49 an hour. Serverless is billed per second of worker time for inference endpoints, and its rates are not price-board rates, so the board does not move on this story — but anyone serving inference on RunPod Serverless is paying the new figures now.

What it costs: a Serverless worker that runs around the clock on a B200 now bills about $7,877 a month at $10.79 an hour, against about $6,307 at the old $8.64 — roughly $1,570 more per always-on GPU. An H100 worker running 24/7 goes from about $3,497 to about $3,935 a month. Serverless is normally bought for spiky traffic, where the per-second billing still beats an idle pod; the rises narrow that advantage at exactly the high end — B200 and H200 workers — where always-on endpoints are most common. This is RunPod's second rise in the recent record (Secure Cloud rose on Oct 14) and it extends the autumn pattern — Nebius on Oct 1, Verda eight times from Oct 23 to Nov 2, SaladCloud on Nov 1: rising prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can also play a part).

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Index, November 2026: H100 to B300
highlights:
Every month we check the public on-demand prices of specialist GPU clouds to set our own: CoreGPU prices every GPU at least 25% below the market median. This is the data behind that number, as listed on November 4, 2026.

## Method

- One on-demand price per provider and GPU, taken from public pricing pages or price APIs. Prices for 8-GPU nodes are divided by eight.
- Specialist GPU clouds only for the median. Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) are listed separately because their prices are 2.5 to 4.5 times higher.
- Monthly cost = hourly price × 730 hours. Prices exclude taxes.

## Median prices by GPU

| GPU | Prices found | Lowest $/h | Median $/h | Median / month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B300 | 8 | 6.60 | 8.98 | $6,552 |
| NVIDIA B200 | 11 | 5.43 | 8.19 | $5,979 |
| NVIDIA H200 | 12 | 2.90 | 4.94 | $3,606 |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | 16 | 1.99 | 3.72 | $2,716 |
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 | 9 | 1.40 | 2.19 | $1,599 |
| NVIDIA L40S | 11 | 0.73 | 1.57 | $1,146 |
| AMD MI325X | 2 | 3.80 | 4.21 | $3,071 |
| AMD MI300X | 4 | 2.59 | 3.22 | $2,351 |

...

## Hyperscalers

On-demand prices per GPU-hour at the largest clouds remain far above specialist clouds: H100 from $6.88 (8-GPU instance divided by eight) to more than $12 depending on the provider, and B300 from $15 to $17.80. Commitments of one to three years cut those prices by 30 to 56%.

## What moved in 2026

- Prices are rising again for flagships. At least one large specialist cloud announced increases of 10 to 26% on H100, H200 and B300 from December 1.
- Clusters cost more than single instances. Multi-node offers are commonly 20 to 50% more per GPU than on-demand single servers.
- Listed is not available. Several providers list GPUs with no deployable region, or “contact sales” for every flagship.
- Fees moved to storage and idle time. Egress is mostly free; stopped-instance storage, public IPs and minimum billing periods are where extra cost appears.

results.title: The Cheapest GPU Rental Right Now (November 2026): What 'Cheapest' Actually Means for H100, H200, and B200
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
- Entering November 2026, the cheapest GPU rental depends entirely on which 'cheapest' you mean: the marketplace/spot floor, a reliable named on-demand rate, or the market median — and they can differ by 2–4x on the same card.
- Cheapest reliable on-demand right now: H100 (80GB) ~$1.99–2.89/GPU-hr (Voltage Park ~$1.99, Thunder Compute ~$2.19, RunPod ~$2.89), H200 (141GB) ~$3.59–4.29 (RunPod ~$3.59, Crusoe ~$4.29), B200 (Blackwell) ~$5.50–6.99 (Lambda is the cheapest reliable on-demand B200).
- Marketplace/spot floors go lower and less certain: H100 asks from ~$1.74 (Vast.ai) and spot ~$1.03 (Spheron), H200 asks from ~$2.25–2.76, B200 single-provider floors as low as ~$3.69 but with availability and trust caveats.
- Market medians are much higher: ~$4.20 H100, ~$5.70 H200, ~$8.19 B200 (Uvik's October index) — so a random provider costs roughly double the floor.
- Hyperscalers (AWS/Azure/GCP) stay ~$7–14/hr for the identical card — you pay 3–6x for the platform, not the silicon.
- The real cheapest option is often NOT renting: below ~40–50% duty cycle a per-token API beats renting metal at any of these rates, because a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it works or not.
- And the direction of travel just changed: with Microsoft and Google pausing capex and chip delays pushing capacity to H1 2027, the price floor that stopped falling in October is now firming — the cheapest rate you see today may be the cheapest you'll see for a while.

...

**The cheapest reliable on-demand rate right now (November 2026):**

- H100 (80GB) → ~$1.99–2.89/GPU-hr. Voltage Park ~$1.99, Thunder Compute ~$2.19, RunPod ~$2.89.
- H200 (141GB) → ~$3.59–4.29/hr. RunPod ~$3.59, Crusoe ~$4.29.
- B200 (Blackwell) → ~$5.50–6.99/hr. Lambda is typically the cheapest reliable on-demand Blackwell.

results.title: The H100 got more expensive · Three Phase. Potentia Intelligence.
results.author: Jose Mir
highlights:
What happened: Nebius raised on-demand GPU prices on October 1, its second hike in about three months. Independent trackers show the same direction across the market.

Why it matters: The bear case on AI infrastructure assumed GPUs lose value fast. Rental rates are the cleanest test of that assumption, and so far the test is failing.

By the numbers:

- Nebius list price for an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour; B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.
- The Ornn H100 index settled at $3.17 on October 23, up about 4% in a month.
